Aboriginal Australians. The indigenous peoples of Australia with one of humanity's oldest continuous cultures, spanning at least sixty-five thousand years. They developed sophisticated kinship systems, sacred sites, and distinctive land management practices while maintaining a profound spiritual connection to the continent. The Aboriginal peoples have inhabited Australia for at least sixty-five thousand years, with some evidence suggesting an even more ancient presence extending over one hundred thousand years. This makes their culture extraordinarily old. They developed complex kinship systems and social structures that organized hundreds of distinct language groups and nations, each with independent governance and law systems. Central to their spirituality is the Dreamtime, sometimes called the Dreaming—a spiritual philosophy that encodes creation narratives, law, geography, and relationships to land in sacred stories and song cycles. In modern times, dot painting emerged as a significant artistic practice, where acrylic dots on canvas represent Dreamtime narratives and sacred geography, gaining international recognition during the twentieth century. The Aboriginal peoples practiced sophisticated land management including cool burning, or controlled fires, to shape ecosystems and improve hunting success. They created detailed rock art across the continent, with some sites showing continuous cultural use for thousands of years. The Aboriginal peoples speak or spoke over two hundred and fifty distinct languages, and many are now extinct or critically endangered, though language revival efforts remain ongoing.
